name: Federalism
summary: Federalism is the theory and advocacy of dividing final authority between member units and common institutions, usually in an entrenched constitution that neither level can alter alone. Its founding arguments hold that this double division, together with checks inside each government and an extended union of many interests, restrains rulers and majorities, lets diverse communities govern themselves, and secures defence and commerce at the centre. It is a structural doctrine and speaks to few questions outside the form and limits of government.
scope: Constitutional federalism as the Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy defines it (a territorial division of power between member units and a common government, including coming-together and holding-together federations), as set out in the texts it names: the Federalist papers of Madison, Hamilton and Jay, Montesquieu on the confederate republic, Althusius, and Mill on federal representative governments. It excludes the US Federalist Party, the states-rights politics of nullification, Proudhon's anarchist federalism and the later European federalist movement except as the Stanford entry reports them, and it answers a statement only where these texts take a position on it.

keyFigures.role: Early modern thinker the Stanford entry calls the father of modern federalist thought.
keyFigures.quote: Althusius, like Aristotle, included non-political units in his federal theory.

sources.title: Federalism, Encyclopaedia Britannica
sources.author: The Editors of Encyclopaedia Britannica
sources.usedFor: Defines federal systems: a perpetual covenant of union in a written constitution, noncentralization so that authority cannot be taken away without common consent, areal division of power, direct lines between citizens and all governments, and the primacy of bargaining among power centres.

clerical-rule.rationale: The Stanford entry says Althusius, the father of modern federalist thought, rejected theocracy and built a non-sectarian, non-religious theory of federations.

common-currency.rationale: Mill counts a single coinage among the arrangements states gain from union and faults the German confederation for never providing one.

confederal-coordination.rationale: Mill and Federalist No. 16 hold that a union acting only through the member governments is a mere alliance that cannot work, and that the federal government must act on individual citizens directly; Britannica makes those direct lines to citizens the mark that separates a federation from a confederation.

consent-of-governed.rationale: Federalist No. 22 says the union must rest on the consent of the people, the original fountain of all legitimate authority, and Federalist No. 39 grounds the Constitution in ratification by the people of each state.

courts-bound-by-majority.rationale: Federalist Nos. 10 and 51 design the union to guard the rights of the minority against a majority united by a common interest, so institutions that do not constrain the national majority contradict them.

decide-locally.rationale: The Stanford entry gives subsidiarity as the guide for dividing power: authority rests with the member units unless a central body would be clearly more effective, and Federalist No. 45 leaves the states the numerous and indefinite powers while the federal ones are few and defined.

direct-votes.rationale: Federalist No. 10 holds that a pure democracy where citizens decide in person admits no cure for the mischiefs of faction, and prefers representation by a chosen body of citizens.

equal-outcomes.rationale: Federalist No. 10 treats the protection of unequal faculties of acquiring property as the first object of government and calls an equal division of property an improper or wicked project that the extended union is less likely to embrace.

ethnic-nation.rationale: The Stanford entry and Britannica present federalism as a way to hold ethnically and culturally diverse groups in one state with territorial self-rule, rather than as a way to unify one ethnic nation.

indirect-election.rationale: Mill praises a federal chamber chosen by the state legislatures as more likely to choose eminent men than a popular election, and Federalist No. 39 describes the Senate as appointed indirectly through the states.

laws-from-scripture.rationale: Althusius's federal theory is described in the Stanford entry as non-sectarian and non-religious, forbidding the state to intervene even to promote the right faith.

member-state-blocks-federal-overreach.rationale: Mill says the power to decide disputes over the federal division must lie in an umpire independent of both governments, Federalist No. 39 puts the deciding tribunal outside the states, and Federalist No. 22 calls a state's right to repeal its part in the compact a heresy.

minority-territorial-autonomy.rationale: The Stanford entry says federal arrangements, including asymmetric holding-together federations, give territorially based minorities self-rule over language and culture within one state, and Britannica says giving fundamentally different groups territorial power bases of their own has strengthened federal systems.

minority-veto.rationale: Federalist No. 22 calls a minority negative on the majority a poison that subjects the sense of the greater number to that of the lesser.

national-church-status.rationale: The Stanford entry says Althusius's federal theory prohibited state intervention even to promote the right faith, which a privileged national church would be.

national-cultural-autonomy.rationale: The Stanford entry describes non-territorial federation after Renner and Bauer, giving dispersed cultural minorities cultural autonomy within one state.

national-self-determination.rationale: The Stanford entry presents federal accommodation of minority nations within one state as preferable to their secession into states of their own.

one-party-rule.rationale: Federalist Nos. 10 and 51 rely on many competing interests and parties checking one another in an extended republic, which an exclusive ruling party would end, and Britannica names a noncentralized party system as the most important support of federal noncentralization.

pool-sovereignty.rationale: Mill says that where the conditions for efficient federal unions exist, multiplying them is always a benefit to the world, and the Stanford entry gives pooling sovereign powers for security and prosperity as a reason for federation.

property-fundamental.rationale: Federalist No. 10 names the protection of the faculties of acquiring property as the first object of government, and the Stanford entry says the Federalists saw federal arrangements as a safeguard against an equal division of property.

regional-powers-revocable.rationale: The Stanford entry defines a federation by a division of power entrenched in a constitution that neither the member units nor the common government can alter alone, Britannica says the authority of the general or state governments cannot be taken away without common consent, and Federalist No. 39 describes the local authorities as distinct and independent portions of the supremacy, not subject to the central legislature at its pleasure.

resist-lawless-ruler.rationale: Federalist No. 28 asserts the original right of self-defense, paramount to all positive forms of government, against the usurpations of national rulers, exercised through the state governments.

right-to-secede.rationale: Britannica makes a perpetual covenant of union the basis of a federal relationship, and Federalist No. 22 calls a state's right to revoke its part in the compact a gross heresy.

second-chamber.rationale: Federalist No. 62 argues for a senate as a second branch, and Mill calls the American two-house design with a chamber representing the state governments exceedingly judicious.

separated-powers.rationale: Federalist No. 51 argues that dividing power between two governments and then among separate departments gives a double security, with ambition made to counteract ambition.

single-common-good.rationale: Britannica says the principles animating federal systems stress the primacy of bargaining and negotiated coordination among several power centres, not a common good set above bargaining.

sovereign-above-law.rationale: Federalist No. 51 says a government must first control the governed and then be obliged to control itself, so a ruler above the law contradicts the design.

state-harmful.rationale: Federalist No. 51 states that government is necessary because men are not angels; federalism divides and checks the state rather than abolishing it.

subordinate-church-to-state.rationale: The Stanford entry says that in Althusius's federal theory accommodation of dissent prevailed over subordinating political powers to religion or vice versa.

suppress-opposition.rationale: Federalist No. 10 rejects removing the causes of faction by destroying liberty as a remedy worse than the disease, and Federalist No. 51 relies on a multiplicity of interests.

total-state.rationale: The Stanford entry says federal arrangements protect individuals against political authorities by constraining state sovereignty, Britannica says federal principles prize dispersed power centres to safeguard individual and local liberties, and Federalist No. 45 limits the national government to few and defined powers.

notes: Later pass under rules 7. The earlier pass answered about 130 statements on the strength of a Wikipedia summary and the remark that adherents differ; those answers were nulled or replaced here, because a structural doctrine that is silent on a statement gives no position (AUDIT_RULES.md section 3). Themes searched: the division of powers and its guard (Stanford entry, Britannica, Federalist Nos. 9, 10, 16, 22, 28, 33, 39, 45, 46, 51, 62, Mill ch. 17, Montesquieu Book 9), majority rule and minority protection, second chambers and indirect election, secession, resistance to usurpation, subsidiarity, minority accommodation, property, defence and commerce. The Federalist essays are used only where they argue about the federal union or the checks that make it work; their republican and presidential claims are not federalism's own and are left out.
